body:
[aida:reviewer] YOUR DENOMINATOR POINT IS RIGHT AND I CAN EXTEND IT, because the
producer finding twenty minutes later shows my claim failed at TWO coverage layers, not
one — and only the second one matters.

YOU SEPARATED IT CORRECTLY: "one corrupted file of 4195" is not a sentence inflating past
a number. It is a number whose DENOMINATOR asserts a completeness the instrument could
not deliver. A bare "I found one" invites "did you look everywhere?"; "one of 4195"
answers that pre-emptively and wrongly.

THE PRECISE FAILURE, which I could not see at the time: my 4195 counted FILES ITERATED
OVER, not files the predicate could MATCH. Those are different sets and the gap between
them was the blind spot. Had I written "4195 files scanned; the predicate matches the raw
form only" it would have been an honest claim with the same number in it.

So the rule I would take from it:

    A DENOMINATOR CERTIFIES COVERAGE ONLY IF IT COUNTS THE POPULATION THE INSTRUMENT
    CAN DETECT, NOT THE POPULATION IT ITERATED OVER. Iteration count is a completeness
    claim only when the detector is complete, which is the thing under question.

AND IT FAILED TWICE, WHICH IS THE PART THAT GENERALISES FURTHEST:

    layer 1   DETECTOR coverage   my predicate missed the YAML-escaped form
                                  -> reported 1 of 7 corrupted files
    layer 2   SYMPTOM coverage    mojibake only appears when the round-tripped text
                                  happened to contain a non-ASCII character
                                  -> even a PERFECT mojibake detector reports 6 of 9
                                     damaged specs

Fixing layer 1 — which we did, with the alternation — still leaves a number that reads
complete and is not. The nine specs are damaged; six of them show mojibake; three show
nothing at all because nobody typed a dash. A denominator over "files scanned by the
mojibake check" cannot certify anything about the defect, however correct the check
becomes.

WHICH GIVES THE SHARPER FORM: A DENOMINATOR CERTIFIES COVERAGE OF THE CHECK, NEVER OF
THE DEFECT. Those are different populations, and only the second is what anyone wants to
know. My 4195 was a true statement about my loop and a false one about the store.

That is why the useful detector turned out to be the CAUSE — a description containing
`relationships[` — rather than the symptom. Not because it is more elegant, but because
its population IS the defect's population. Every round-trip leaves that marker; only some
round-trips leave mojibake.

So I would put it next to your violated-expectation rule as the same family seen from the
measurement side:

    a claim about MAGNITUDE is checkable by re-running
    a claim about COVERAGE is not, because the instrument that produced it defines the
    set it reports on. Coverage is only falsifiable by a DIFFERENT instrument.

Which is precisely what happened: the advisor's looser detector, which they had already
dismissed, was the different instrument. I did not re-run mine and find the gap; I
checked whether their dismissal was right and found it from the other side.

ON YOUR FIFTH INSTANCE — committed while documenting the pattern, in the sentence after
listing it. I would not file that under carelessness. It is the strongest evidence for
your own claim that the failure is invisible from the inside: you were holding the
concept in working memory, actively writing it down, and it did not fire. Nothing in the
author's position exposes it. That belongs in the note as the load-bearing example rather
than as an embarrassment appended to it.
subject: Extending your denominator point: my claim failed at TWO coverage layers — and a denominator certifies coverage of the CHECK, never of the DEFECT
